summary.text: A nearly 8-year-old intact male mixed-breed dog weighing 9.20 kg, abandoned by its owner, was found and referred to an animal shelter in Iran. It was unconscious, unable to move, depressed and severely obese, with marked abdominal distension and icteric mucous membranes at the initial examination. Heart rate was 105 beats per min and within normal limits, with mild tachypnea (43 breaths per min) and a rectal temperature of 39.60 ˚C.

Blood samples were collected. The complete blood cell count showed leukocytosis (49.90 × 10³ µL^-1), thrombocytopenia (101 × 10³ µL^-1) and increased red cell distribution width (14.90%). Biochemistry showed hypertriglyceridemia (455 mg dL^-1), elevated ALT, AST and ALP, and cholesterol lower than the normal range. The blood smear showed neutrophilia, band cells, metamyelocytes, nucleated red blood cells, a moderate regenerative left shift and anisocytosis.

Referral to a veterinary hospital for advanced diagnostic imaging was scheduled, but the dog experienced sudden death before departure from the shelter. A postmortem necropsy immediately followed and found an extremely enlarged, yellowish, icteric liver with extensive fat damage and abnormal kidneys with nodular lesions. Fatty liver was strongly suspected, and liver and kidney samples were preserved in formalin for histopathology.

Histopathology confirmed severe fatty degeneration of the liver, with fatty vacuoles replacing the parenchyma, congested central veins and sinusoids, and hepatocyte necrosis. The kidneys showed degenerative and necrotic changes, glomerulonephritis, tubular lesions, hyperemia and hemorrhage. The authors attribute the death to the severe form of the disease, very late referral and renal involvement.

Comparisons with cited dog and cat studies, fold differences from a cited study, and general statements about hepatic lipidosis are not patient facts.
